title: The news
hookLine: how to take in the world without despair: Jesus and the tower of Siloam, Epictetus and what's in our power
tomorrow: a herdsman told a temple to turn off its music. why?

lines: A FLOOD, A CRASH, BEFORE BREAKFAST.
cards: The feed refreshes: a flood, a crash, a cruelty, all before breakfast. Luke's Gospel has people arriving with the news of their own day.
Some tell Jesus about Galileans killed by the Roman governor, Galileans "whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices."
And Jesus brings up another headline himself: eighteen people killed when the tower in Siloam fell on them. Two disasters, one cruel and one an accident. What do you do with news like that?

teach.h: THE NEWS IS NOT A VERDICT ON THEM.

teach.b: First he refuses the easy reading: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."
The victims weren't worse people. The news isn't a verdict on them.
Then he turns the listeners back to their own lives: change your own heart. Christians hear in it a call to turn toward God, not to judge the people in the headline.
A neighbor tradition says something close in its own words.

teach.h: SOME THINGS ARE IN OUR POWER.
teach.b: The Stoic teacher Epictetus opens his Handbook: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Our judgments and our choices are ours; the world's events are not.
Here's what they share: both send you back from the headline to what's yours to do.

teach.h: REPENTANCE FOR ONE, REASON FOR THE OTHER.
teach.b: And the honest difference: Jesus turns the listener toward God and repentance, a change of heart. Epictetus turns you toward your own judgments, with reason as the guide.
Awake to the world, not drowning in it.

how: Christians read Luke 13 as a warning against blaming the victims of disaster and a call to turn their own lives toward God; readers of Epictetus sort what is in their power from what is not.

games.q: after a disaster, a friend says the people hit 'must have done something to deserve it.' what's Jesus's answer in Luke 13?
o: no: the victims weren't worse; the news turns you back to your own life.
partly: disasters can be warnings aimed at the people they strike.
it's a mystery, so better not to say anything to your friend.
games.why: suppose ye that these were sinners above all? I tell you, Nay.

practice: Pick one set time tomorrow for the news, and only one, and decide how long it gets. Then bring one of today's headlines to mind, name one small thing in it that's in your power, and let the rest go by with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The news: the world taken in at a set time, without judging its victims and without drowning. Siloam and the Handbook.

orig.note: Greek: a change of mind or heart; the New Testament's word for repentance.

carryVoice: Here's the line: awake, not drowning, eyes open to the tower and feet on your own ground. See you out in the world.
